replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it doesn't see that word at all.

It sees three chunks: **"un"**, **"believ"**, **"able"**.

That's because LLMs don't read words — they read **tokens**.

A token is a fragment of text, somewhere between a character and a word. GPT-4 uses a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. Common words like "the" get their own token.

Rare or long words get split into pieces. Numbers, punctuation, even spaces — all tokenized separately.

[EX]The word "bank" becomes one token. But "tokenization" splits into "token" + "ization." And the sentence "I went to the bank" is ambiguous even before the model starts thinking — the tokenizer just chops it up; it doesn't know if "bank" means a riverbank or a financial institution.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokens are the actual units an LLM reads — not words, not letters, but learned fragments mapped to numbers.[/KEY]

Before we move to what the model *does* with those tokens, let me check your footing:

[Q]
A word like "strawberry" might be split into multiple tokens. Why does this matter for how an LLM processes text?
A) It means the model reads faster because shorter chunks are easier
B) It means the model might not "see" a whole word as one unit, which can cause errors on tasks involving individual letters
C) It means rare words are ignored entirely
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it probably doesn't see one word — it sees **three pieces**: "un", "believ", "able."

That's because the first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — not words, not letters, but chunks that the model learned are useful during training.

A token is roughly 3–4 characters on average. GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of about 100,000 possible tokens. Every token gets converted to a number, and that number points to a location in a high-dimensional mathematical space.

[EX]The sentence "I love AI" might become tokens [40, 1842, 9552] — three numbers that the model can actually do math on. The words are gone; only the numbers remain.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization is the process of converting your text into numbers before the model ever "thinks" about your prompt.[/KEY]

Here's what's important: the model has no idea what a word *means* the way you do. It only knows patterns — which number-sequences tend to follow which other number-sequences, based on billions of examples from training.

[Q]
What is a token, exactly?
A) A copy of your prompt stored in the AI's memory
B) A chunk of text converted to a number the model can process
C) A full word that the AI looks up in a dictionary
ANS: B
[/Q]

B) A copy of your prompt stored in the model's memory
